children: Industrial production in Germany unexpectedly shrank in July, driven by sharply lower activity in the country's troubled auto sector.

Output fell 1.1% on month after a flat reading in June, the country's statistics agency Destatis said Monday. That marked the strongest decline since August last year. Economists polled last week by The Wall Street Journal had expected a 0.1% rise.

The industrial sector in Europe's largest economy has mostly defied fears that the surge in energy prices since the start of the Iran conflict would hurt activity. Production was 0.4% higher in May through July than in the prior three-month period, and factory orders have risen for three straight months.

Production has been resilient as Asian rivals were hit harder by the closure of the Strait of Hormuz, and companies stockpiled German goods in anticipation of the higher costs and supply issues due to the war. Companies also felt more of the effect of fiscal stimulus from the German government on defense and infrastructure investments.

However, warnings continued to emerge from the car sector, where production fell 9.2% on month in July. Some of that decline was due to the retooling of a plant for electric-vehicle manufacturing, Destatis noted.
The board of German auto giant Volkswagen last week approved doubling already severe job cuts to 100,000 as it faces stiff competition from China, alongside U.S. tariffs.
Low water levels in Germany's rivers caused by recent heatwaves are also expected to have hampered production in August.
The data serves as a reminder of how fragile the recovery of the German economy is, Carsten Brzeski, economist at Dutch bank ING, said in a note to clients.

"Looking ahead, the war in the Middle East, which is slowly turning into a forever war, keeping oil prices at elevated levels, as well as the likely upcoming shock of higher gas prices in the next heating season and renewed trade tensions, pose risks to the German outlook," he said.
